en: The Philippines has a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons instead of four temperate seasons.
Red soil found in some Philippine provinces gets its distinct color from a high iron oxide content.
Pumice is a highly porous volcanic rock containing many trapped air bubbles that allow it to float on water.
Morning dew forms on grass when invisible water vapor in the cool night air condenses into liquid drops.
Venus reflects so much sunlight that it appears as the brightest morning star in the eastern sky.
The Pleiades star cluster, locally known as Moroporo, becomes visible in the evening sky to signal the dry season.
The Moon's gravitational pull creates high tides that regularly raise the ocean water level in coastal towns.
Heavy rains wash loose volcanic ash down mountain slopes, creating fast-flowing, destructive mudflows called lahars.
Cumulonimbus clouds grow tall and dark, bringing heavy rain and thunderstorms during hot Philippine afternoons.
Quartz is a hard, glassy mineral that makes up the clear grains of sand found on local beaches.
The Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, causing the Sun to appear to move across the sky.
Typhoons produce strong winds that can uproot large trees and tear roofs off houses in coastal communities.
